USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Use the Trump-Xi G20 dinner to open a time-bound negotiation, not to settle. Hold the existing $250B tariff architecture in place and make any delay of the January 1 List 3 hike to 25% contingent on a short, enforceable work plan covering IP/tech transfer, not another purchase-pledge communiqué. Do not add the threatened ~$267B list this week, and do not roll back or lock in purchase commitments until China puts dates and verification on structural changes.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is modest, not existential. The Section 301 case remains live—USTR’s March finding on IP/forced tech transfer, Lists 1–3 now covering ~$250B, and Lighthizer’s late-November assessment that China “has not fundamentally altered” those practices. That is a real interest at stake, but the US macro core is still intact: industrial production is slightly higher, Michigan sentiment is 97.5, and CPI is contained. The bite is concentrated and political: US goods exports to China fell ~15% from July to November (EXPCH $10.15B → $8.65B); soybean sales to China are down ~94% on 25% Chinese retaliation, with storage overflow and only a fraction of the $12B farm-aid package paid out; VIX is ~18.5 versus ~12 in June; the dollar is firmer and CNY has weakened to ~6.95. Those are farm-belt and market-volatility costs, not a recession. China is under more cyclical pressure (IP y/y 6.0 → 5.4, reserves down ~$56B, import compression), which is leverage, not a reason to declare victory. Action should stay near zero because the May 19 “trade war on hold” joint statement collapsed ten days later when Washington judged purchase language insufficient, and China’s recent 142-point list is again being read in Washington as thin on timetable and enforcement. Escalating into the G20 (auto-hiking List 3 or launching List 4) would hit more consumer-facing imports, invite broader Chinese retaliation against remaining US export channels, and waste the first leader-level opening since the November 1 call. Unconditional rollback or purchase concessions would repeat May and spend the January 1 deadline for another unenforceable truce. Negotiate: explore a pause of the scheduled hike only against a dated, verifiable structural track, and keep tariffs as the backstop if talks fail.
key_factors: G20 Trump-Xi meeting is the first leader-level opening since the Nov 1 call
List 3 is scheduled to rise from 10% to 25% on Jan 1, 2019, with a further ~$267B list threatened
Section 301 IP/tech-transfer complaints remain unmet (Lighthizer: no fundamental change; 142-point Chinese list judged thin)
US farm/export pain is acute (EXPCH -15%; soybean sales to China ~-94%) while core US activity and sentiment are still solid
China is the more cyclically strained party (slower IP, CNY ~6.95, reserve drain), so US leverage is usable if not spent cheaply
May 19 truce collapsed within 10 days — purchase pledges without enforcement are not a settlement

sources_cited.excerpt: USTR Section 301 report finds China's IP/tech-transfer practices unreasonable; Trump directs tariffs, a WTO case, and investment restrictions.
US-China joint statement: China agrees to significantly increase purchases; Mnuchin says trade war is on hold. Truce collapses on May 29 when the White House proceeds with Section 301 tariffs.
List 3 takes effect at 10% on ~$200B; China retaliates 5–10% on ~$60B; combined US Section 301 coverage ~$250B. Rate scheduled to rise to 25% on Jan 1, 2019.
Trump and Xi phone call on trade; agree to meet at the G20 in Argentina.
US goods exports to mainland China fell from $10.15B (July) to $8.65B (November), about -14.8% over the window.
VIX close 18.49 on 2018-11-28 versus the low-12s in early June (~+45%), consistent with elevated market stress into the G20.
CNY weakened from ~6.40 in early June to 6.9534 on 2018-11-28 (~+8.6%), a competitiveness offset for China and a pressure gauge.
China industrial production y/y index eased from 106.0 (July) to 105.4 (November), a modest real-economy slowdown on China's side.

Officials preview a possible G20 truce: delay the Jan 1 hike to 25% and hold the extra ~$267B list while talks continue; Kudlow says a deal is possible but Trump is 'perfectly happy to stand on his tariff policies'; China's 142-point list judged to lack timetable and enforcement.
Federal data through mid-October: US soybean sales to China down 94% from last year's harvest; China was the largest market for one of America's largest exports.
USTR: additional tariffs on ~$200B effective Sept 24 at 10%, rising to 25% on January 1, 2019.

Lighthizer report: despite tariffs on ~$250B, China 'has not fundamentally altered its unfair, unreasonable, and market-distorting practices.' Most likely G20 outcome described as a cease-fire into a more intense negotiating phase.
